b: Elizabeth Reid, vice president and head of Search at Google, said in a podcast interview published on November 19, 2026 that people "don't want purely AI, they want AI in the web," and that there is "less interest in sort of very shallow surface level reciting" while content built on expertise, personal experience and in-depth research still finds an audience. Speaking on FOMO Sapiens, a podcast hosted by Patrick J. McGinnis, Reid named preferred sources and the ability to follow creators as ways Google is connecting publishers with users as AI Mode and AI Overviews reshape Search, described how videos rank higher in India than in the US for the same query, and said AI Overviews were held to the quality bar of featured snippets when they launched. She offered no figures on traffic, clicks or revenue.

Google's head of Search told a podcast that people want AI answers mixed with links to the web, and that pages which only restate simple facts are drawing less interest than content with real expertise or experience behind it. That matters to publishers and creators, because Reid pointed to preferred sources and creator follows as Google's answer to them, not to traffic numbers, while independent studies covered by PPC Land have measured fewer clicks from AI search. What changes is the framing: Google is describing a web that survives inside the AI answer, and Reid gave no data on how much of that web still gets visited.

The episode, titled "S15E8 Elizabeth Reid, VP of Search at Google on How AI is Changing Search," appeared on McGinnis's YouTube channel on November 19, 2026. It runs about 35 minutes. According to the closing credits, FOMO Sapiens is recorded in New York City; McGinnis says in the introduction that he coined the term FOMO. The channel lists about 1,640 subscribers, and the podcast page shows 510 episodes.

Reid joined Google in 2003 as the first female engineer in its New York office, according to McGinnis's introduction and the episode description. She worked on Google Local, which the description calls "an early foundation of Google Maps," and, in the host's words, has since 2021 "led the team's rebuilding search with AI at the core." The description adds that she was named to the TIME100 AI list in 2026.

This is not the first time Reid has used a podcast to describe where Search is going. PPC Land covered her appearance on the Access podcast in March, where she pointed to audiences moving toward podcasts and creators; her April conversation on Bloomberg's Odd Lots, in which she described people stating their real problem instead of translating it for a computer; and her June interview on AI Inside, where she argued that personalization pushes results toward niche publishers and that paywalls predictably reduce traffic. In October 2025, she told a Wall Street Journal event that revenue with AI Overviews had been relatively stable, as fewer clicks on some queries were offset by more searches overall.

FOMO Sapiens describes itself as a show about how "entrepreneurial thinkers" find the courage to build exceptional lives, not a search industry podcast. Much of it covers Reid's career, her leadership approach and her daily use of Google's tools. But about 18 minutes in, McGinnis asked the question that publishers have been asking for two years: with so much happening inside Google's own pages, "how are these companies going to survive in this in this new age of of AI powered um search."
"AI in the web": what Reid told publishers
Reid did not answer in terms of revenue or referrals. She answered in terms of demand.
"So um what we generally see is that people don't want purely AI, they want AI in the web," she said. "They do want um specific kinds of content on the web and not as much others, right?"
Her example of the second kind was blunt. "If you built a whole web page for which the purpose was to tell you the time zone in Japan, it's just not that useful, right?"

Fashion was her example of the first. "The the the people that tend to turn to AI for fashion advice are the set of people who didn't spend any time on fashion previously, right?" she said. "If you used to spend an hour scanning fashion blogs once a week, you that's not replaced by something else. Um you actually still care very much to hear from other people."

From there, Reid set out the kind of content she believes keeps its audience. "There's communities you want to be a part of. There's influencers you look up to, right? Um there's folks who go in-depth on a topic and really research it and study," she said. "And so we see that there's still a lot of demand for content um that brings your personal expertise that brings um you know your unique experiences to that that brings in-depth research."

The other side of that line was stated just as directly. "So there's less interest in sort of very shallow surface level reciting. let's hope you win, you know, the lottery of ranking," Reid said. Her test for which side a page falls on was a question: "would you as a human want to read that, right? Um, or is it just a means to an end?"
She summarized Google's position as "a web forward experience that brings the best of the web and the best of AI together."

Reid then named the mechanisms. "We're also experimenting with new ways to en enable um those publishers and creators to further connect with the users in this world," she said. "So things like preferred sources if you really love to hear on this topic about leadership from [FOMO Sapiens] and now somebody asked a question well can [FOMO Sapiens] rank higher for them because they've expressed a preference in that. Um can you follow creators? Can you do that?"

The goal, she said, is "to really try and and and nurture and give give value when people have felt that connection with particular publishers and creators," and to make it "easier for you to hear from the voices you love and trust."

Neither feature is new, and PPC Land has tracked both. Google launched preferred sources in Top Stories on August 12, 2025, in English and only in the US and India. In December 2025, Nick Fox, Google's senior vice president of Knowledge and Information, said people who select a preferred source click through to that site twice as often, as the feature went global for English-language users. Google brought preferred sources into AI Overviews and AI Mode on May 27, 2026, when it said more than 345,000 unique sources had been selected; by August 20 the count had passed 600,000. On October 15, Google said use of the feature had grown more than 7x since the start of the year, without a baseline, and began testing clickable creator names on AI Mode video results that lead to Search profiles.

Following is a separate system. Creator follows arrived in Google Discover, the personalized feed in the Google app, when Google added them on September 17, 2025, and Search profiles, which gather a publisher's or creator's content in one place, went live in the US on June 6, 2026 with eligibility thresholds of 100,000 followers on YouTube, Instagram or X, or 300,000 on TikTok. At that launch, Google said changes to a Search profile do not affect ranking in Google Search or Discover, with following adding a signal for the Discover feed. Reid's phrasing in the interview, "can you follow creators? Can you do that?", described a direction of travel more than a finished product, and she did not say whether following would ever carry the ranking effect she attributed to preferred sources.

McGinnis's question was about money: how publishers would earn when readers no longer leave Google. Reid's reply addressed what kinds of content people still want. It did not address how many of them still click, or what a publisher earns when its content is used inside an AI answer without a visit.

That gap is where most of the evidence PPC Land has covered sits. In a preregistered field experiment with 1,100 US participants, people moved entirely into AI Mode for a week clicked through to outside websites 18.8 percentage points less often than people on standard Google Search; they also visited news sites, Reddit and Wikipedia less often. A randomized study by researchers at the Indian School of Business and Carnegie Mellon found outbound organic clicks fell 39.8% when an AI Overview appeared. Ahrefs data linked AI Overviews to a 58% lower click-through rate for top-ranking pages. On October 29, Reddit chief executive Steve Huffman named AI Overviews and AI Mode as the biggest factor behind declining search referrals to Reddit, a site built on exactly the community content Reid described as still in demand. Google has disputed several such measurements; in July, Nick Fox said AI features in Search send billions of clicks to websites every week, without a comparison figure.

Reid's image of shallow pages hoping to "win" the "lottery of ranking" also touches a sore point for small publishers. At a Web Creators Summit in Mountain View on October 29, 2024, Google Search executives apologized to 20 small and independent publishers for algorithm changes that cut their traffic, according to an attendee's account. Is a page's depth something Google can reliably detect, and does detecting it translate into visits? The interview did not take up that question.

Reid opened the search part of the conversation with how people phrase queries now that AI can interpret them. "I think what you see is that people start asking much more of what they really care about, right?" she said. "They didn't take their thing and boil it down to some simplistic thing and then have to do all the work on top. So the questions get much more hyper specific. They reveal the constraints that matter to you, what you really want out of the choices you're making."
Google tracks this through data and user research, she said. "The questions keep changing. The questions get longer. um the questions get more specific um in what they need."

She traced the pattern back to her work on local search. People first asked "yellow page type questions," then expected opening hours, until "one time we looked up and they were asking when does the breakfast menu at this particular McDonald's close." The difference now, according to Reid, is that "you don't just have to match a web page or match a business. You can pull information and synthesize and reason about the information to pull together an answer."

Asked for tips, Reid gave an example that the episode also uses as its opening clip. "Don't just ask where can I get Halloween costumes. Ask I want a Halloween costume for my 11-year-old girl in this theme delivered tomorrow that'll keep her warm. Ask that question." When McGinnis summarized it as "be very specific," she corrected the emphasis: "Be as specific as matters to you."

Google has published figures that point the same way. In May, Shivani Mohan, Google's vice president of data science for Search, said the average AI Mode query was three times the length of a traditional search query, as AI Mode passed 1 billion monthly users; she repeated the point to advertisers in an Ads Decoded episode on October 28. On the same day, Alphabet said its year-over-year Search query growth rate was the highest in five years, while Search revenue rose by just $79 million on the second quarter. Longer queries carry more information about intent, which is why the length matters to advertisers bidding on them. Whether longer queries are as valuable per search to Google is a separate question that Alphabet's disclosures do not answer.

Reid also said people adapted faster than Google expected. Moving a weather button on the results page can take "like 6 months" before people notice, she said, "but but the rate at which people started asking longer questions the rate at which once because once they did it like it worked so well they did it more they told their friends etc."
The search box, the plus box, Search Live and Lens

Reid's main tip for users concerned input, not phrasing. "I think one tip that many people don't do is that they're still in all I can give is text, right?" she said. "You actually have like with the plus box that's now in the new search box, like you can upload files that you want to ask that question. You can upload multiple images that you want. And so you can actually talk with search live and have a back and forth conversation, not just type things in."

At I/O on May 19, Google introduced a redesigned search box that expands for longer queries and accepts text, images, files, videos and Chrome tabs. Reid called the entry point "the plus box." Search Live, the voice and camera mode inside AI Mode, reached all US users in English in September 2025 and expanded to more than 200 countries and territories on March 26, 2026. The episode description calls it "a spoken back-and-forth inside AI Mode."

Reid described the search box as one of two ways Google teaches people what is possible. "We added lens, we added AI mode, we added the plus box to allow these ones," she said. The other is suggestions inside the conversation: "We will often say would you like to know more in some form, right?" Those prompts, she said, are tailored to the answer rather than repeated after every response, and "it doesn't have to be a disruptive promo."

Lens drew some of her most specific comments. When it took off, people began asking questions they had never typed, about a plant or "that cool bag that somebody else was doing," and then began "combining the picture with a question about the picture." She uses it daily: the day before the recording, she said, she photographed a page of her daughter's workbook and asked Lens for 20 fill-in-the-blank questions to help her study for a quiz. In July 2025, Robby Stein, vice president of product for Google Search, said visual searching on Google had grown 65% year over year. For marketers, the shift toward images, files and voice changes what a query contains: a photographed product or an uploaded document arrives with no keyword at all.

Asked what listeners could try in the coming week, Reid named two features. "I think users could try search live which allows you to have a conversation about the information on from within AI mode," she said, adding that "some of them have probably never used lens."
India and the US: same product, different ranking
McGinnis asked whether Google is the same product in the US and in Kenya. Reid said the core product is the same but behaves differently by market, and gave India as the example.

"The use of voice is much heavier in India than in the US," she said. "Another example in there is that people's interest in videos is much higher in India than in the US." The ranking consequence followed: "Even though both the US product and the India product will surface videos and images and websites and whatever else the how high the videos will rank in India will be different than how high they'll rank for the same query in the US."

That is a direct statement from Google's head of Search that the same query can return a different mix of formats by country, with video placed higher in India. Reid gave no measure of the difference, did not say which query types are affected, and did not name other markets with similar adjustments. When Google launched AI Mode in India as a Labs experiment in June 2025, it said more people used Lens each month in India than in any other country.

Reid said AI makes this kind of adjustment easier, because "it's not just about the language it's also like the same concept is different." Her example was emergency numbers: 911 in the US is not the number in the UK. The outcome, she said, is a product that "you would still recognize it as Google search but it would behave subtly differently."
How Google staged AI in Search, and the featured snippet bar
McGinnis put to Reid that a hallucination costs Google more than it costs newer AI companies, because of the trust Google has built. Reid answered with the order in which Google introduced AI.

She recalled that in the early days Sundar Pichai, chief executive of Google and Alphabet, "coined the phrase bold and responsible." Then she described three stages. "So first it was an opt-in experiment for those that wanted to be on the cutting edge so we could learn and they wanted to take advantage of the powers but they knew what it was," she said. "And then we rolled out AI overviews, but you still had the rest of the search page before we got in. And then AI mode was a click away, so you could still have that."

The quality standard was the part with the most specific claim. "We have traditional things like web snippets that we used to have. We call them featured snippets that show up at the top where you you expand the answer around," Reid said. "Um what was the quality bar? We held that to we held [AI Overviews] to match that quality bar at time of launch and the quality has only improved since then."

She added that Google deliberately traded fluency for accuracy. "There's inherently a tension between creativity and sort of factuality right the more the more you encourage it to just sort of always say something and be unique and different the more likely it is to not say the right thing," she said. "So we say we're going to give up on some of that fluidity and some of that creativity because people are going to come to us for that high quality and and factuality."

Reid did not say how the featured snippet bar is measured, what score AI Overviews achieved against it, or how often either feature is wrong. The launch record is mixed. On May 30, 2024, weeks after AI Overviews reached US users, Google published a post acknowledging odd and inaccurate AI Overviews, including an answer about eating rocks drawn from a satirical article, and announced restrictions on satirical queries, forum content and health topics. Google opened AI Mode as a Labs experiment on March 5, 2025, when AI Overviews already reached more than 1 billion users. In the field experiment covered by PPC Land, participants moved into AI Mode rated Google as less trustworthy than those on standard Search.

Reid also argued that perfection was never the benchmark. "Google search was never perfect, right?" she said, pointing to knowledge panels and to Wikipedia, which people once doubted and now treat as trusted. "In our mind like trust is hard fought and easily lost and so we have to keep that paramount."

Her personal test, she said, sits on top of "all the careful [evals] we run and studies we do and extreme testing." It is whether she could defend a launch to people she knows. "On the one hand a lot billions of people are going to use this product so it darn better be good and two those billions of people include my mother my child my next door neighbor," she said. "I don't want to ship something that I that I can't be proud of in front of my mother, right?"
In the closing "FOMO 4" round, McGinnis asked for a Google Search trick most people have never heard of. Reid chose information monitoring.

"We have this new feature around information monitoring that lets you go say, 'Keep me updated about things,'" she said. Reid uses it for her town's events, after repeatedly missing a local fair, for new plays, and for industry news. "What's going on in the industry that isn't just, you know, sort of keyword matching? It's sort of like Google Alerts 2.0," she said. "That it's too much work to ask every day, but you'd love to know when the world changes."

Delivery runs through notifications and AI Mode. "You can get a notification, then you get the response in in AI mode," Reid said. "But you can just go to search and say like keep me updated on this and it will say would you like me to set up an alert and and and work with you on it."

At I/O in May, Google said these background information agents would launch first for AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, and on June 12 they went live for AI Ultra subscribers in all AI Mode languages. By November 16, Google's holiday guide and help page described ticket and price monitoring in AI Mode without naming any paid tier. Reid presented the feature as available, without mentioning a subscription, and did not say when or whether the requirement changed.

For brands and publishers, a monitoring task replaces a habit that used to generate repeat visits or repeat searches. A user who once checked a retailer's restock page or a local news site every few days can instead receive a synthesized update from Google. Reid's own framing, monitoring "that isn't just, you know, sort of keyword matching," points to a system that reads the web on a user's behalf and reports back inside AI Mode.
Subscriptions, AI literacy and the free product

McGinnis remarked that the tools are free. Reid added a qualification. "There's there's there's a Google AI subscription in general that allows you on search and other ones to like use the more powerful models," she said. "But yes, search is really designed for everyone to be able to just use and ask the hardest questions."

The split is visible in recent launches. On November 10, Google began rolling out Gemini 4 Carbon in AI Mode for Google AI Ultra subscribers only, describing it as its strongest model. The announcement named no route to that model in AI Mode for subscribers on the cheaper AI Pro plan, and none for users without a subscription.

Asked which question about AI nobody is asking, Reid named literacy. "I don't think we're talking enough about AI literacy," she said. People once had to learn how to search with keywords, she noted, and now need to learn "how to get the best out of AI how to use the tools well." She pointed to Google's own programs, including an AI certificate through Grow with Google, but said "we as society should be thinking about how are re-equipping ourselves and the next generation of people to live in this world."
Reid declined to give the size of her organization. "We don't share the numbers," she said, describing it only as "a large team."
How the features work, as Reid described them
Reid described four flows in the interview. According to her account:
Uploads through the plus box. The new search box includes a "plus box" that lets a user "upload files that you want to ask that question" and "upload multiple images" alongside a question.
Search Live. From within AI Mode, a user can "talk with search live and have a back and forth conversation, not just type things in."
Information monitoring. A user tells Search "keep me updated on this"; Search replies with an offer to "set up an alert"; updates then arrive as a notification, and the response opens in AI Mode.

In-flow suggestions. After an answer, Search may ask whether the user wants to know more "about this very specific thing," or ask for missing details, such as "what your trip is for and who you're going with."
Reid gave no eligibility rules, markets, age limits or subscription requirements for any of the four in the interview.

The interview restates Google's public position on AI search: the answer sits on top, the web sits inside and below it, and the content that keeps attention is personal, expert or community-driven. For publishers, that position is now attached to specific mechanisms, preferred sources and follows, which favor brands with an established audience. A site that readers have never chosen gains nothing from a preference signal, and Search profiles launched with thresholds set at six-figure social followings.

The commercial side was absent from the conversation. Reid did not mention advertising once. On October 28, Google extended ads in AI Mode to 10 more countries, including India, with Brazil, Mexico and the UK planned for the fourth quarter and multiturn ads launched in the US; existing Search, Shopping and Performance Max campaigns are eligible automatically, without a separate opt-out. The longer, more specific queries Reid encouraged are the same queries on which those ads now run.

India's video ranking difference is a small but concrete disclosure for anyone planning content by market. The featured snippet comparison is a quality claim without published numbers. And information monitoring, presented as a convenience, carries the zero-click search pattern beyond a single results page, since the update arrives inside AI Mode rather than on the site where the news first appeared.

The interview leaves several things unaddressed. Reid gave no figures for traffic sent to publishers, for the effect of preferred sources or follows on rankings in AI Mode, for the size of the India ranking difference, or for how AI Overviews measure against featured snippets. She did not say whether information monitoring now requires a subscription.

Who: Elizabeth (Liz) Reid, vice president and head of Search at Google, interviewed by Patrick J. McGinnis, host of the FOMO Sapiens podcast.

What: Reid said people "don't want purely AI, they want AI in the web," that interest is falling in shallow pages while expert, experience-based and community content keeps an audience, and that preferred sources and creator follows are Google's tools for connecting publishers with users. She said videos rank higher in India than in the US for the same query, that AI Overviews were held to the featured snippet quality bar at launch, and described the plus box, Search Live, Lens and an information monitoring feature she called "Google Alerts 2.0." She gave no traffic, click or revenue figures and did not discuss advertising.
When: The episode was published on YouTube on November 19, 2026.
Where: On FOMO Sapiens, a podcast recorded in New York City and published on YouTube and podcast networks.

Why: Publishers and marketers are weighing Google's account of AI search against independent studies showing fewer clicks from AI Overviews and AI Mode, as Google expands ads inside AI Mode and adds features, such as monitoring alerts, that keep users inside its own interface.
